title: Canada’s AI opportunity depends on graduates who can apply AI responsibly in the real world
summary: Canada’s AI opportunity depends on graduates who can apply AI responsibly in the real world | Pearson plc
body_markdown:
24 Nov 2026 published at 14:00 PM GMT


*New Pearson and Amazon Web Services report calls for stronger connections between postsecondary learning and work to turn Canada’s AI higher education leadership into better conduits of workforce readiness*


**TORONTO, Nov. 24, 2026 —** A new report from[Pearson](https://plc.pearson.com/) (FTSE: PSON.L), the world’s lifelong learning company, and Amazon Web Services (AWS) finds Canada has many of the components needed to succeed in an AI-enabled economy, but must turn growing AI use and experimentation into practical capabilities graduates can demonstrate in the workplace.


[AI Readiness: Building the Bridge from Higher Education to Work in Canada](https://www.pearson.com/content/dam/global-store/global/resources/ai-readiness/CA-AI-Readiness-EN-1.pdf) examines how Canada can build on its AI ecosystem, strong postsecondary institutions, and tradition of work-integrated learning as AI adoption accelerates across the economy.


**AI adoption is rising, but uneven**


Research shows the Canadian labour market is already being reshaped by AI:


- **19.2%** of Canadian businesses used AI to produce goods or deliver services in the 12 months prior to April/May 2026.
- **25.2%** of businesses planned to use AI over the next 12 months following July 2 to August 6, 2026.
- **35.9%** of Canadian workers aged 15 to 69 reported using generative AI at work.


Yet AI use alone is not evidence of AI readiness. The report identifies four capabilities graduates need to succeed in an AI-infused economy, striking a balance between technical and human skills: functional AI proficiency, strategic intelligence, ethical stewardship, and critical human skills such as adaptability, communication, and judgment.


Helping students build those capabilities also requires faculty to have the confidence, support, and disciplinary context to integrate AI meaningfully into their teaching, keeping learning firmly at the center. Educators need to develop their own AI fluency and literacy to better empower them to design learning experiences that help students practice responsible AI use authentically.


**Jessica Biga-Wadstein, Country Head, Pearson Canada, said:** “Canada already has strength in AI research, education, and work-integrated learning to lead, but access alone won’t prepare graduates for what comes next. To close the gap between potential and practice, we need to support faculty in designing meaningful opportunities for students to build experience using AI, challenge its outputs, and make accountable decisions in real-world settings. That means educators and employers working more closely together to make AI readiness something graduates can demonstrate and verify.”


**Five actions to build AI readiness in Canada**


The report identifies five evidence-based priorities for Canadian institutions and employers:


1. Define capability before choosing technology, with clearer expectations for what graduates should be able to demonstrate.
2. Move from experimentation to program-level alignment, connecting AI use with curriculum and assessment.
3. Build authentic AI practice into learning through employer-informed projects, simulations and work-integrated learning.
4. Invest in human judgment, including faculty support, safe infrastructure and responsible AI governance.
5. Learn at the pace of change through stronger, continuous feedback between educators and employers.


The report builds on Pearson and AWS’s global AI Readiness research and six-point Friction Framework, combining that global perspective with recent Canadian research and interviews across higher education, industry, and the AI ecosystem for the Canadian context.


Learn more at[https://www.pearson.com/power-of-learning/ai-readiness.html](https://www.pearson.com/power-of-learning/ai-readiness.html) .
